description_full: Tyson Foods, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as a food company worldwide. It operates through four segments: Beef, Pork, Chicken, and Prepared Foods. The company processes live fed cattle and hogs; fabricates dressed beef and pork carcasses into primal and sub-primal meat cuts, as well as case ready beef and pork, and fully cooked meats; raises and processes chickens into fresh, frozen, and value-added chicken products, including breaded chicken strips, nuggets, patties, and other ready-to-fix or fully cooked chicken parts; and supplies poultry breeding stock. It also manufactures and markets frozen and refrigerated food products, including ready-to-eat sandwiches, flame-grilled hamburgers, Philly steaks, pepperoni, bacon, breakfast sausage, turkey, lunchmeat, hot dogs, flour and corn tortilla products, appetizers, snacks, prepared meals, ethnic foods, side dishes, meat dishes, breadsticks, and processed meats under the Tyson, Jimmy Dean, Hillshire Farm, Ball Park, Wright, Aidells, Gallo Salame, ibp, and State Fair brands. The company sells its products through its sales staff to grocery retailers, grocery wholesalers, meat distributors, warehouse club stores, military commissaries, industrial food processing companies, chain restaurants or their distributors, live markets, international export companies, and domestic distributors who serve restaurants and food service operations, such as plant and school cafeterias, convenience stores, hospitals, and other vendors, as well as through independent brokers and trading companies. Tyson Foods, Inc. was founded in 1935 and is headquartered in Springdale, Arkansas.

financial_summary: Tyson Foods, Inc. is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $20.7B market cap on $54.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 4% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 9% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.55× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.6% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
